About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Japanese Years 11–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Japanese Years 11–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Japanese Years 11–13 is proposed to be
made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section
90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Japanese Years 11–13 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from 1
January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

Students are taught how language reflects identity, relationships, values, beliefs, and
worldviews. Through Japanese, students gain insights into the histories, traditions,
innovations, and contemporary experiences of Japan. They explore how people
express ideas, maintain relationships, participate in society, and share knowledge,
while developing an appreciation of the diversity within and across Japanese-

and cultures, students deepen their understanding of different ways of thinking,
communicating, and making sense of the world. They are provided with opportunities
to develop intercultural understanding through examining how language and culture
influence practices and perspectives.

Texts are used as resources for learning, enabling students to develop linguistic,
cultural, and sociolinguistic knowledge, and to apply this learning in their own
language production. Meaning is communicated through spoken, written, interactive,
and multimodal forms, and learners develop increasing capability to interpret, create,
and respond to texts across modes. Decisions about text selection and use are
integral to unit design and support the meaningful enactment of the teaching
sequence.
Language learning is a gradual, long-term process that develops through ongoing
practice and exposure. Progress is supported when learners take risks and recognise
that making mistakes is a natural and valuable part of acquiring a new language. A
collaborative and supportive learning environment further strengthens this
development, enabling students to engage actively, build confidence, and grow their
language capabilities together.
